item.title: Asian Games: Pakistan extend winning runs in hockey and squash; kabaddi team bow out. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan’s hockey and squash teams kept their momentum going at the Asian Games on Thursday, while the country’s kabaddi campaign ended in disappointment and boxer Maria Rind bowed out.

Pakistan hockey maintained their winning run with a 3-0 victory over China at the Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium, recording their third win in as many matches.

China had the early chances but failed to make the most of two penalty corners, while Pakistan squandered two of their own.

The national side came out all guns blazing in the second quarter, earning two penalty corners before being awarded a penalty, which Abu Mahmood converted.

Sufyan Khan then struck five minutes later from a penalty corner before Hannan Shahid added a field goal two minutes before half-time.

Both teams traded chances in the second half but could not breach the goal.

Sufyan has now scored five goals in three matches, all from penalty corners. Pakistan next face Malaysia in their Pool B fixture on Saturday.

In squash, Noor Zaman and Mohammad Ashab Irfan cruised into the quarter-finals with comfortable victories at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena.

Third-seeded Noor swept aside Kuwait’s Ammar Altamimi 11-4, 11-9, 11-4 in 26 minutes, while Ashab downed Saudi Arabia’s Mohammad Al Alnafsan 11-9, 11-3, 11-5 in 36 minutes.

Pakistan’s top-ranked Noor faces Chi Hin Henry Leung on Friday, while Ashab, ranked 49th in the PSA standings, takes on India’s Veer Chotrani for a spot in the semi-finals.

Earlier, Asim Khan and Mehwish Ali survived a scare, coming back from a game down to reach the mixed doubles quarter-finals.

The pair lost the first game 11-8 to Japan’s Naoki Hayashi and Erisa Sano but kept their nerve to take the second 11-10, before regrouping to claim the decider 11-4, to wrap up the triumph in 39 minutes.

The other Pakistani team of Nasir Iqbal and Sehrish Ali crashed out after losing their last-16 clash to Hong Kong’s Ming Hong Tang and Ka Yi Lee 11-2, 11-6.

Pakistan’s kabaddi campaign ended with a heavy 51-30 defeat to Iran in their final Group B match at the Tokai Citizen Gymnasium.

Iran led 20-14 at the interval and pulled away in the second half, outscoring Pakistan 31-16.

Iran’s dominance showed in the stats: 41 outs, eight all-out points and two bonus points, while Pakistan managed 23 outs, four bonus points and three super-tackle points.

Pakistan, who had won their opening two fixtures against Malaysia and Nepal, finished with two wins and two losses.

Iran and Thailand advance to the semi-finals from Group B, while India and Chinese Taipei moved ahead from Group A.

At the Nishio Gymnasium, Maria Rind was eliminated from the women’s 51kg boxing competition, stopped by Mongolia’s Yesugen Oyuntsetseg at 0:31 of the third round.

Maria had been down once in the second before two more knockdowns in the third prompted the referee to halt the contest. She trailed on all five scorecards after two rounds.

On the track, Faiqa Riaz failed to qualify from her heat, finishing fifth in 11.96 seconds. The national champion missed out on the semi-finals by 0.48 seconds, behind Pui Kei Chen of Hong Kong.

In the pool, Pakistan’s struggles continued as Mishael Aisha Hayat Ayub and Hamza Asif failed to advance from their respective heats at the Tokyo Aquatics Centre.

Competing in the women’s 50m freestyle, the 24-year-old Mishael finished third in her heat in 30.04 seconds, behind Laos’ Tamsiri Niyomxay (29.80) and Turkmenistan’s Valeriya Mirenskaya (29.11).

Overall, she finished 30th out of 35 swimmers, with Chinese Taipei’s Pei-yin Liu the last to qualify in 25.64.

Hamza finished last in his heat of the men’s 50m butterfly with a time of 26.37 seconds, 3.14 seconds behind Bahrain’s Mikhail Arkhangelskiy, who won heat 5.

Overall, the 20-year-old finished 36th among 44 competitors.

The slide continued in fencing as Mohammad Waqas and Abdul Musawir both lost all six of their bouts in the men’s epee individual at the Aichi Sky Expo Hall.

Waqas, 25, opened with a 5-3 defeat to Kyrgyzstan’s Uulu Ilim Bakytbek, then lost three bouts 5-2 against Qatar’s Abdulrahman Aljadra, Japan’s Masaru Yamada and Mongolia’s Munkhkhasar Ulaankhuu. He produced an improved display against Bangladesh’s Md Imtiaj but still lost 5-4, before closing with another 5-2 defeat to Hong Kong’s Ho Tin Ng.

In Pool 5, Musawir was first beaten 5-3 by Gandul Batbyamba, before Singapore’s Simon Renjie Lee downed the 26-year-old 5-2. Hong Kong’s Hoi Sun Fong then brushed him aside 5-1, before Uzbekistan’s Meyirkhan Timurov, Saudi Arabia’s Khalifah Khalil Alomairi and the UAE’s Khalifa Alzarooni all handed him 5-2 defeats.

More defeats followed in table tennis as Mohammad Khan and Taha Bilal both lost their fixtures 4-0 at the Sky Hall Toyota.

Mohammad was routed by Thailand’s Thitaphat Preechayan, while Bahrain’s Rashed Rashed overpowered Taha.

At the Nagaragawa International Regatta Course, Pakistan’s Asad Iqbal finished second in Final B with a time of 7:06.72, behind India’s Ajay Tyagi, leaving him eighth overall.

item.title: One more Fatima Sana, and Pakistan would have gold. [ dawn ]
item.description:
EARLY on Tuesday morning, while most of the nation was asleep, Pakistan beat Bangladesh to win bronze in women’s cricket at the Asian Games in Japan — the country’s first medal in the event since gold in 2014, and its second medal of the ongoing edition overall. It came against an opponent that had denied them at this same stage three years ago, and had beaten them by 23 runs at the T20 World Cup in July. Pakistan had also just lost to Sri Lanka in the semi-final, as they had in the Asia Cup less than 10 days earlier.

This time, they won. Captain Fatima Sana led her team to the podium — arguably the first tangible reward of her captaincy — much as she has led them through most of the days before it.

Nature of the game

Cricket is technically a team sport, but in practice it behaves like several individual sports wearing a trenchcoat. Master your own discipline — batting, strike bowling, spin — and you can often get away with being less than complete elsewhere (fielding aside). Still, modern cricket rewards being a fortified jack of some trades over a master of one — a bowler who can bat a little, rather than merely survive at No. 11, is simply more useful.

Because individual brilliance carries so much weight in this sport — think Glenn Maxwell’s 200 against Afghanistan, or Ben Stokes’ century at Headingley in 2019 — it’s easy to turn cricketers into heroes.

Every team wants to be a well-oiled machine — clinical fielding, wickets falling on schedule, batting picking up where bowling leaves off. But nothing replaces the pull of a single, standout act of brilliance.

That’s especially true in Pakistan, where the simplest explanation is that the system hasn’t learned to make goodness routine — masla system mein hai (the problem is in the system), as the local diagnosis goes for every sporting failure. Because Pakistan’s brilliant individuals rarely get the infrastructure to sustain themselves, their brilliance never regulates into something as boring as consistency.

It also makes each instance feel larger than life — a heroic knock in England, Fakhar Zaman’s Champions Trophy final century, Naseem Shah’s sixes against Afghanistan, Razaullah’s recent rearguard action on debut.

Factor in the women’s game, where whatever the men lack is lacking tenfold, and every flash of brilliance there is mathematically more pronounced.

Even accounting for all of that, it’s hard to overstate what Fatima Sana is doing right now.

The numbers

In 2026, Fatima Sana has scored 540 runs in women’s Twenty20 Internationals — the most by any Pakistan batter — at an average of 45 and a strike rate close to 150, second only to India’s Shafali Verma among batters past 400 runs this year.

She has hit more sixes than any team-mate, and in matches Pakistan has won, her average rises to 55.8. She has also been Pakistan’s leading wicket-taker for the year with 31 scalps in 21 matches at 15.6.

The more striking shift isn’t the volume, it’s that she has gone from a bowler with handy batting contributions to a player who could make the side on either skill alone, and done so while carrying the added weight of captaincy.

Learning the job under fire

Fatima made her international debut in 2019 in Potchefstroom, where Pakistan routed South Africa for 63 under Sana Mir, the legend she shares half her name with, who took 4 for 11 that day. Fatima struck on her third ball. In 2021, she became the first Pakistani woman to win the ICC’s Emerging Cricketer of the Year award.

She was named permanent captain in August 2024, ahead of the T20 World Cup, succeeding Nida Dar, Bisma Maroof and Sana Mir — three stalwarts of the women’s game in Pakistan.

But her first taste of leadership came earlier, in a New Zealand ODI in late 2023, when Nida was ruled out with concussion symptoms after a Sophie Devine blow. Fatima, 22 then, walked out at 35-4 — her only prior fifty a solitary knock from earlier that year — and made 90 not out in a 90-run stand with Natalia Parvez, while her opening spell had New Zealand pinned at 13-2.

Pakistan lost by one wicket after a tight lbw shout with no DRS to review it. It was a preview of what her captaincy would often look like.

None of this is to suggest Fatima is the side’s only class act. Sadia Iqbal was briefly the world’s No. 1 bowler in WT20Is. She and Nashra Sandhu, who took the first six-wicket haul by a Pakistan player in an Asia Cup match this month, both sit in the top 10 of the rankings. Opener Muneeba Ali has anchored the side for years despite a recent dip, and a cohort of recent U-19 graduates, alongside young talents like Shawaal Zulfiqar and Aroob Shah among them point to depth ahead.

A captain who keeps doing the improbable

It’s a risky habit, romanticising a captain who keeps punching above her weight in a team sport, and it’s one I’ve had to check myself on every time I write about her — because I don’t want captain and InshaAllah to be Pakistan’s model. But Fatima has pulled off the rescue job often enough, made runs no one else wanted to make, that “punching above her weight” may no longer be the right description.

She might just be that good.

Her first match as captain came at the 2024 T20 World Cup against Sri Lanka, where she top-scored with 30 off 20 at No. 7 and had Chamari Athapaththu out for six, a player-of -the-match performance that led Pakistan to a 31-run win.

Later that tournament, Fatima’s father died in Karachi and she flew home mid-competition, returning to cry through the national anthem before Pakistan’s match against New Zealand. A year later, in a promotional video for the 2025 Women’s ODI World Cup, she recalled his last words to his doctor: “Make me better quickly. My daughter is playing the World Cup. I want to watch her play.”

In April 2025, Pakistan won all five matches at the home World Cup qualifiers under her captaincy; she was player of the match against Thailand (62 not out and 3-39) and finished the tournament just one wicket behind top-scorer Hayley Matthews. That May, she hit the fastest fifty in Women’s T20I history, one that came off 15 balls against Zimbabwe.

The near-misses count too. Earlier this year in South Africa, she walked in at 64-6 and made 90 off 41 — arguably the best innings by a Pakistani this year — before being bowled off the last ball, still visibly hungry for more.

In this month’s Asia Cup semi-final, her unbeaten 47 and four wickets weren’t enough to stop a third straight semi-final loss to Sri Lanka. And against England at last year’s ODI World Cup, in a tournament Pakistan finished winless, she bowled Nat Sciver-Brunt with a nip-backer and had Heather Knight lbw to leave England seven down — only for rain to wash the match, and the points, away.

The real conversations

That rainy day in Colombo may sum up Fatima’s captaincy so far; Pakistan do everything right, she leads them through it, and something still falls short.

There are real conversations to have — about whether she should be batting higher, about not being the only one producing these performances, about a bronze in a four-team-realistic field being, in some sense, an under-achievement.

But Pakistan can’t afford to keep overlooking greatness when it’s standing in front of them —a captain who hangs her head after a match-defining 47 because she wanted more, who stood for the anthem days after bidding the final goodbye to her father. One more Fatima Sana, and Pakistan would have gold.

item.title: Getting support for the Rohingya. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is encouraging to see Bangladesh taking active measures to put renewed pressure on the international community to help resolve the Rohingya crisis, and facilitate their safe, voluntary, and dignified return to Myanmar.
During his visit to New York for the UN General Assembly, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman sought continued international cooperation for a sustainable solution to the crisis during a meeting with UN Secretary-General’s Special Envoy on Myanmar Julie Bishop. Bangladesh also co-hosted a high-level side event on the Rohingya crisis, aimed at renewing international political and humanitarian support and strengthening accountability efforts.
These are undoubtedly important steps. For years, Bangladesh has carried an enormous humanitarian responsibility while the Rohingya have remained trapped in prolonged displacement. Now, more than nine years after the massive influx of 2017, the crisis cannot be allowed to become an accepted permanent reality.
International concern has produced humanitarian assistance, statements, and diplomatic engagement, but these have yet to deliver the outcome Bangladesh and the Rohingya need most: A safe and sustainable return home.
As Bangladesh has rightly emphasized, repatriation cannot simply mean crossing the border. Myanmar must provide conditions that guarantee security, rights, and dignity.
That is why sustained international pressure is essential. The UN, regional powers, and other influential countries must do more to address the conditions that have prevented meaningful repatriation. Myanmar must also face continued pressure to create an environment in which the Rohingya can return voluntarily and with confidence in their future.
Bangladesh should continue using every diplomatic platform available to keep this issue at the forefront of international attention. The current efforts are a welcome indication that we are not prepared to let the crisis fade from the global agenda.
We have wanted successful repatriation for years; it is time to finally make it happen. Continued diplomacy must now translate into coordinated international action, concrete pressure and, ultimately, a dignified return for the Rohingya to their homeland.

item.title: Ending our culture of impunity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The deaths of two people in separate road incidents in Dhaka this week have exposed a long-standing problem that goes beyond reckless driving or unfortunate accidents: The persistence of a culture in which accountability too often comes after tragedy, if at all.
24-year-old construction worker Mehedi Hasan Mir was killed by a car that ran over him on a footpath, with a 16-year-old detained for the incident. In a separate case, 50-year-old Meherun Begum with hearing disabilities was killed by a DNCC garbage truck while collecting recyclable materials.
These cases underline just how vulnerable ordinary citizens remain in spaces that should be safe. They also raise questions about who is responsible when vehicles are operated without adequate safeguards, when drivers fail to exercise due care, or when public authorities do not sufficiently protect people working or living around their operations.
We have seen too many incidents followed by familiar promises of investigation and action, only for public attention to move on. That cannot be allowed to become the end of the process.
Every death on the road must lead to a credible investigation, clear determination of responsibility and, where warranted, meaningful legal consequences.
Accountability must apply equally, regardless of wealth, family connections, or institutional position. The same principle must govern public bodies such as city corporations; government vehicles and private cars alike must be subject to the law.
Ending impunity also requires prevention through stricter enforcement, safer vehicle operations, proper driver training, better monitoring, and protection for pedestrians and vulnerable workers.
A city cannot call itself safe when people can lose their lives simply by resting on a footpath or collecting recyclable materials.
Justice must be ensured for these deaths -- and the countless other similar tragedies that have plagued our streets for too long.
More importantly, however, the system must be made into one that ensures that fewer families are left seeking this kind of justice in the first place.

item.title: Bangladesh’s next leap?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Over the years, I have sat on many sides of the same economic story.
I have seen it through the eyes of a microfinance borrower, a migrant, a family separated by borders and, today, a technology entrepreneur building in Silicon Valley.
Those experiences have convinced me of something: Bangladesh’s next great financial transformation will not come from one technology. It will come from connecting technology to the realities of ordinary people.
My first exposure to that reality came through Grameen Bank.
Working in microfinance taught me that financial inclusion is not simply about giving someone access to money. It is about giving people the ability to make decisions, take control of their economic lives, and create opportunities that previously seemed out of reach.
I learned an important lesson there: Capital is powerful, but knowledge and access determine how effectively people can use it.
Years later, at the UN migration agency, the International Organization for Migration (IOM), I encountered another side of the equation.
I worked directly with migrants and saw the human story behind migration statistics. People weren’t simply “sending remittances.” They were working thousands of miles from home to pay for a child’s education, build a house, support parents or create a better future for their families.
A remittance is therefore not just a financial transaction. It is a sacrifice converted into hope.
Then, working in the visa section of the Swedish Embassy, I spent years speaking with migrants and families navigating the complexities of moving across borders.
That experience taught me something else: Behind every application, transaction, and statistic is a human being trying to move forward.
Today, from Silicon Valley, I see a fourth piece of the puzzle.
I see what happens when software, artificial intelligence, and modern financial infrastructure are designed to remove friction from everyday life.
And it raises a question I cannot ignore: What if Bangladesh could combine the lessons of microfinance, the realities of migration, and the power of AI to fundamentally change what happens to every taka that comes home?
That is the opportunity in front of us.
From remittances to wealth
Bangladesh has become a global remittance powerhouse.
Millions of Bangladeshis work abroad and send money home, with remittances reaching approximately $35.6 billion in FY2025-26.
But sending money internationally remains surprisingly expensive and complicated.
A worker in Riyadh, New York, or London may initiate a transfer that passes through several financial intermediaries before his family receives taka in Rangpur, Sylhet, or Barisal.
The technology of the internet has made information instantaneous. Yet moving money can still feel like sending a letter by courier.
We should ask a more ambitious question: What if the world’s financial infrastructure moved at internet speed?
This is where Web 3.0 and regulated digital-dollar settlement become interesting. Stablecoins such as USDC or USDT are digital currencies designed to maintain a stable value, typically by being backed by reserves such as US dollars or highly liquid assets. In simple terms, they are a way of representing dollar value digitally and moving it over the internet.
Their more important long-term potential may be as financial infrastructure, rather than as speculative instruments.
The United States has now formally recognized this potential. The GENIUS Act, signed into law in 2025, established a federal regulatory framework for payment stablecoins, including requirements around reserves, redemption, and oversight.
Traditional financial institutions are also building in this direction.
JP Morgan, for example, has launched JPM Coin as a bank-issued digital deposit token that allows institutional clients to move and settle US dollars on blockchain networks around the clock. Other major financial institutions, including Bank of America, Citi, and Goldman Sachs, are also exploring dollar-denominated digital settlement infrastructure.
The distinction is important: Bank-issued deposit tokens are not necessarily the same thing as stablecoins such as USDC.
But they demonstrate something significant: The world’s largest financial institutions increasingly see blockchain-based digital money and programmable settlement as an evolution of financial infrastructure.
For ordinary people, the concept can be much simpler: A dollar with an internet connection. The customer doesn’t need to understand blockchain. They shouldn’t have to.
What matters is whether regulated technology can make money move faster, more transparently, and at lower cost, while maintaining the protections people expect from the financial system.
Dollar in. Taka out. A regulated institution initiates the transaction abroad.
Digital settlement infrastructure moves the value. A licensed Bangladesh-side institution receives it, converts it into taka, and delivers it to the recipient’s bank or approved mobile financial account.
The technology does the complicated work behind the scenes. The customer gets a faster, simpler experience.
And this is not merely theoretical. An IMF study estimated roughly $2 trillion in stablecoin transactions during 2024, with approximately $633bn in North America and $519bn in Asia and the Pacific.
Relative to economic size, activity was particularly significant in Latin America and the Caribbean and in Africa and the Middle East.
For Bangladesh, however, this must not become an excuse to abandon prudent regulation. The question is not whether Bangladesh should blindly embrace Web 3.0. It is whether Bangladesh can responsibly experiment with regulated digital settlement for remittances.
One corridor. Licensed institutions. Full KYC and AML controls.
Strict transaction limits. Transparent reporting. Mandatory conversion into taka with Bangladesh Bank firmly in control.
The objective is not less regulation. It is better infrastructure underneath effective regulation.
Faster money is only half the revolution
My experience at Grameen Bank keeps bringing me back to the same realization: Access without understanding is incomplete inclusion.
Imagine a migrant worker asking an AI assistant in Bangla: “আমি প্রতি মাসে ৫,০০০ টাকা সঞ্চয় করলে পাঁচ বছর পরে কত হবে?”
Imagine a mother receiving a remittance asking: “How much should I save for my children’s education?”
Imagine a first-time investor asking: “What is a bond? What is a stock? What is inflation?”
Today, we can build AI systems that answer these questions instantly, patiently, and in the user’s own language.
This is more than a chatbot. It could become a personal financial tutor for an entire country. It could teach budgeting, savings, investing, insurance, debt management, and fraud prevention.
With agentic AI, people can eventually do more than ask questions. AI agents can help execute financial tasks and, under carefully defined controls, potentially transactions.
But this is precisely where we must be careful. The same AI that can democratize financial knowledge can democratize financial fraud.
AI can generate convincing scams, impersonate voices, create fake documents, manipulate users, and produce confident but unsuitable financial advice.
So AI-powered financial inclusion must be built with safety by design, not safety as an afterthought.
That means strong data-privacy protections, clear disclosure when people are interacting with AI, continuous fraud monitoring, suitability and risk checks before financial recommendations, audit trails for AI-driven actions, and human oversight for high-impact decisions.
AI should explain before it acts. And when the stakes are high, a human should remain in the loop.
The goal is not to replace financial professionals or regulators. It is to give them better tools -- and give ordinary people better access to knowledge.
The smartphone could become more than a wallet. It could become Bangladesh’s most accessible financial classroom.
Imagine connecting the two
This is where the vision becomes bigger than payments.
Imagine a Bangladeshi worker in New York sends $500 home. The transaction moves through a regulated Web 3.0 settlement rail. A licensed institution in Bangladesh converts the funds into taka. The family receives the money.
Then the AI financial assistant asks: “Would you like to see what you could save over the next year?”
It helps them build a budget. It explains compound interest. It identifies potential financial risks. It teaches them how to avoid scams. And, where appropriate, it explains regulated savings and investment products.
The journey changes from:
Remittance → Spending
to:
Remittance → Financial Literacy → Saving → Investing → Wealth Creation.
That is the transformation I believe Bangladesh should pursue.
The diaspora is our global economic network
My years working with migrants changed how I think about the Bangladeshi diaspora.
We often talk about migrants as a source of foreign currency. But that is only one dimension of their value.
They are workers, entrepreneurs, investors, professionals, consumers, and bridges between Bangladesh and the global economy.
They don’t just send money. They send knowledge, aspirations, relationships, and eventually, capital.
What if Bangladesh built financial infrastructure designed around that reality? What if a Bangladeshi in New York could send money home and, through the same trusted ecosystem, understand how to invest in a Bangladeshi business?
What if someone in London could support their family while also building a long-term investment portfolio connected to Bangladesh?
What if remittances became the gateway through which the diaspora participated more deeply in the country’s economic future?
Then the objective changes. We are no longer simply trying to increase remittances. We are trying to increase the economic value created by every remitted dollar.
Build the future. Don’t wait for it
We don’t need to transform the entire financial system tomorrow. We can start with a controlled experiment.
Take the United States-Bangladesh corridor.
Bring together Bangladesh Bank, licensed banks, remittance providers, regulated digital-dollar infrastructure companies, and technology platforms.
Create a sandbox. Set strict limits. Monitor every transaction. Measure settlement times, costs, FX spreads, formal-channel usage, AML outcomes, and customer experience.
For AI, measure something equally important: Accuracy, fraud detection, consumer complaints, inappropriate recommendations, data protection, and human-override rates.
Then let evidence -- not ideology -- determine what happens next.
If it works, scale it. If it doesn’t, learn from it.
The most innovative countries in the world aren’t necessarily those that remove every rule. They are the countries that learn how to innovate safely.
From microfinance to AI
When I look at my own journey -- from Grameen Bank, to working with migrants at IOM, to sitting across from families at the Swedish Embassy, and now building technology in Silicon Valley -- I see a common thread.
The technology has changed dramatically. The human aspirations have not.
People still want the same things.
A better life. A safer future. An education for their children. A home. Financial security. An opportunity to build something of their own.
What has changed is our ability to build systems capable of helping millions pursue those goals simultaneously.
Microfinance showed the world that financial inclusion could start at the grassroots.
Mobile financial services showed Bangladesh that technology could put financial tools into the hands of millions.
AI now gives us the possibility of putting personalized financial intelligence into the hands of everyone.
And modern digital settlement gives us the possibility of moving money across borders with dramatically less friction.
Put those pieces together, and something much bigger emerges.
Bangladesh does not need to become the world’s Web 3.0 capital. It needs to become a country where:
That is the vision. A future where the Bangladeshi worker abroad doesn’t simply send money home. He sends the opportunity home.
Where the family receiving that money doesn’t simply spend it. They learn, save, and invest.
Where the smartphone doesn’t simply transfer money. It teaches a child about compound interest.
Where financial infrastructure doesn’t simply process transactions. It helps build trust.
And where Bangladesh doesn’t simply consume the next generation of financial technology. It helps build it.
My experiences in Bangladesh, with migrants and with families, taught me something more important: The best technology is not the technology that looks most futuristic. It is the technology that makes ordinary people’s lives better.
Bangladesh has the talent, the diaspora, the scale, and the entrepreneurial energy to lead this next chapter. We don’t need to wait for the future of finance to arrive.
We can build a Bangladesh that is ready for it -- and help shape what that future looks like.
And after generations of Bangladeshis sending money home, perhaps it is finally time for the money to arrive before the tea gets cold.
Farihan F Rahman is a Bangladeshi technology entrepreneur and founder of InveStar, a Silicon Valley AI wealth-tech company. He is a Director of Startup Grind, the world’s largest startup community, a Draper Champion, and Perplexity AI fellow.

item.title: In the global staging of a refugee crisis, language is sovereign. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Language is slippery, often subversive. When Burma became Myanmar in 1989, this was the ruling junta’s most overt disavowal of the colonial past. In striking out Britain’s name for the nation, the military attempted to put forth a new image.
The old name, derived from the dominant Bamar ethnic group, was replaced in a sort of semantic trick. It suggested the nation, this new Myanmar, welcomed all ethnic groups composing the vast country.
Junta control would go on to ebb and surge amid the stuttering thrust of “true democracy” -- as it does, as it will -- but that new name, the national veneer, the nom de plume to dissemble the nom de guerre , was largely accepted. Most of the world today indeed recognizes the name “Myanmar.”
Manipulations of language have proven effective tools for the authority of Myanmar. The explosive consequences of these actions are laid bare in decades of ethnic cleansing and genocide of the minority Rohingya, over a million of whom now seek refuge in neighbouring Bangladesh.
While linguistic exploitations by Myanmar state perpetrators have been scrutinized, however, a parallel adaptation of language concerning the refugees by humanitarian systems and host nations has been largely overlooked, despite this language increasingly compromising the welfare of the Rohingya.
Re-evaluating the standard lexicon of the aid system now is critical. Bangladesh presides for the first time over the 81st session of the UN General Assembly which opened in September and has high-level conferences and general debate scheduled this week.
At the helm of the UNGA is foreign minister Khalilur Rahman, selected in a historic election this past June, who was previously the High Representative on Rohingya Issues during the interim government of Bangladesh.
This is an unprecedented position with high potentiality, given Khalilur Rahman’s expertise (coupled with Bangladesh’s election of new Prime Minister Tarique Rahman) but will the old rhetoric staging the refugees’ condition -- ineffective, often counterproductive -- be finally retired?
Sweeping language abounded in the listed objectives for the UN’s first high-level conference on the Rohingya and other minorities of Myanmar which took place in September 2025. The UN organ published aims of the conference ahead of last year’s meeting, including to “review the overall [Rohingya] crisis and address its root causes,” the aspirational outcome of which being “a comprehensive, innovative and concrete plan for a sustainable resolution of the crisis.”
The head of Bangladesh’s interim government at that time, Muhammad Yunus, put forth an address at that meeting which included a seven point plan concerning the Rohingya in Bangladesh. The entirety of this address, however, did not include the word “refugee” to describe those displaced under conditions of war and genocide.
And though this was yet another appeal by the Bangladesh administration to the global community for aid concerning the Rohingya, the displaced population in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh (composing the largest camp system in the world) are still not recognized de jure by the Bangladesh government via the term “refugees.”
Instead, they are designated “Forcibly Displaced Myanmar Nationals” (FDMN). Bangladesh also continues to abstain from ratifying the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol, a decision that allows the nation to circumvent certain mechanisms of international refugee protection frameworks and law.
Systemic manufactures disguised as intrinsic flaw
Yunus also stated during that September 2025 UN meeting: “Bangladesh is a victim of the crisis. We are forced to bear huge financial, social, and environmental costs. Criminal activities…threaten our social fabric.”
The portrayal of Bangladesh as a “victim” of a crisis, closely juxtaposed with the formulaic generalization of the Rohingya as “criminal,” is also a calculated linguistic -- ideological -- construction.
Notably, the Rohingya are largely financially supported by international donor groups and other foreign governments (covering over 90% of the Rohingya Joint Response Plan in 2025), and Bangladesh has in fact experienced local economic development in Cox’s Bazar from the influx of foreign aid and personnel.
Moreover, Bangladesh bars the Rohingya from legal higher education or employment opportunities, so the refugees are often forced into markets which exploit Rohingya workers for further economic gain.
The language of criminality as it pertains to the Rohingya, then, presents a sustained and systemic manufacture as an intrinsic attribute. Bangladesh has in fact extracted a certain legitimacy and foothold through perpetuated Rohingya containment.
Furthermore, the language of a helpless saviour, a victim of an unsavory population, as reinforced by Bangladesh’s highest office, has been co-opted by other host nations to devastating effect.
Harms of international aid community language
The characterization of the refugees in the greater international aid community must also be assessed. The words “burden” and “burden-sharing” (a term which has its genesis at the inception of the UNHCR) are near-universal phraseology for deliverables related to refugee solutions development.
Though this language has been modified at times through the expanded term “burden and responsibility sharing” (this term appearing in documents concerning the high-level UN conference on the Rohingya), the diction invariably confounds sustainable solutions development.
Expediency, asymmetrical compromise, and generalization become the dominant undercurrents of conversation, often influencing safety and longevity considerations. The refugee community of Cox’s Bazar thus become the load to cast off, an onus of little apparent value (humanistic, capitalistic, all that lies between).
Host nations certainly require assistance of international bodies to manage massive refugee populations. These bodies must be cognizant of the unintended effects of modern aid solicitation language.
A major component of this aid solicitation language is made manifest by the international community’s recurring description (see Yunus’ aforementioned speech) of the Rohingya refugees’ condition as a “crisis.”
The hackneyed term is somewhat a misnomer when describing the state of refugees. The connotations of “crisis” elicit ideas of acute, natural phenomena: Successions of events by which victims and witnesses alike are vulnerable, with this state of “crisis” materializing no obvious perpetrators.
In recent headlines relating to the Rohingya, ample mention is made of a humanitarian disaster, a population that is aid-dependent. Less emphasis and fewer details concerning the Myanmar authority are expounded upon, leaving the refugees an abstraction isolated from the political and historical events which made them refugees.
Retiring a philosophy of rhetoric
The first high-level conference on the Rohingya at the UN concluded last year with further aid commitments from a few nations, though funding remains significantly short of targets. The issues facing Rohingya in Bangladesh also persist, with no real success in developing repatriation pathways or resettlement policies for the refugees.
Notably, however, there is fertile ground for reform at the moment. Bangladesh has transitioned from its interim government to a new administration on the wings of renewed democratic process and promise for inclusive national change. Moreover, with Khalilur Rahman at the helm of the UNGA, he will oversee numerous agendas, including the old call for a “sustainable resolution” for the ongoing displacement and genocide of the Rohingya.
There will be speeches insisting that promises and pledges translate this time to “real action,” and by this these parties will gesture to policy change. Inaction stems, though, not only from empty words. The recycling of an old lexicon, an entire philosophy of influential rhetoric, must be retired.
Farihah Ahmed received her MFA in Writing from Columbia University. She is the founder and director of RoVena, a global civil society organization which advocates for Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh.

item.title: Pakistan women seal Asian Games bronze after win over Bangladesh; India take gold. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Umm-e-Hani’s superb three-wicket spell and captain Fatima Sana’s counter-attacking 45 helped Pakistan beat Bangladesh by 31 runs and claim the bronze medal in the women’s cricket competition at the Asian Games in Nisshin, Japan on Tuesday.

Umm-e-Hani conceded only 10 runs in her four overs, including a wicket-maiden, as Pakistan overcame Bangladesh’s early resistance to restrict them to 114 for seven after posting 145 for eight.

The medal is Pakistan’s third in the women’s cricket competition at the Asian Games, following gold-medal triumphs in 2010 and 2014.

It also marked a measure of redemption for Pakistan, who had lost the bronze-medal match to Bangladesh at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou.

Pakistan had been in danger of posting a modest total after collapsing from 46 without loss to 67 for five, but Fatima changed the course of the innings with an aggressive 30-ball 45.

The captain, who struck three fours and three sixes, added 67 from 43 balls with Aliya Riaz to take Pakistan towards a competitive total. Aliya contributed 25 from 22 balls, including two sixes and a four.

Fatima’s innings was particularly significant in the context of her prolific year. She entered the match as Pakistan’s leading run-scorer in women’s Twenty20 internationals in 2026 and took her tally to 540 with Tuesday’s knock. She also remains Pakistan’s leading wicket-taker in T20Is this year.

Earlier, Pakistan made a steady start after Fatima won the toss and elected to bat, with Gull Feroza and Shawaal Zulfiqar putting on 46 in 6.4 overs.

Gull struck six fours in her 23-ball 31 before Nahida Akter ended the opening stand, while Shawaal made 17 from 27 balls.

Bangladesh then seized control, taking five wickets for 21 runs to leave Pakistan struggling at 67 for five. Fatima and Aliya, however, rebuilt the innings before accelerating after Pakistan reached 90 for five in 15 overs.

Fatima struck Rabeya Khan for six before both batters cleared the ropes against Sanjida Akter in the 17th over. Pakistan added 55 runs in the final five overs, although Bangladesh hit back by taking two wickets and conceding only seven in the final over.

Nahida, Shorna Akter and Ritu Moni claimed two wickets apiece for Bangladesh.

Pakistan’s defence began emphatically as Umm-e-Hani and Tasmia Rubab reduced Bangladesh to 20 for three inside five overs.

Umm-e-Hani struck in her first over, removing Juairiya Ferdous, before Tasmia dismissed Dilara Akter for 12. Umm-e-Hani then removed Sobhana Mostary early in the fifth over.

All three catches in the opening exchanges were taken by Saira Jabeen, including a spectacular effort at the cover boundary to dismiss Dilara.

Bangladesh’s hopes rested on captain Nigar Sultana and Sharmin Akhter, who added 47 for the fourth wicket. Nigar made 25 off 30 balls with three fours, while Sharmin remained unbeaten on 46 from 45 balls, hitting four fours.

But with Bangladesh requiring more than 10 runs an over at the halfway stage, the task became increasingly difficult. Ayesha Zafar trapped Nigar leg-before in the 14th over, before Umm-e-Hani and Fatima struck in successive overs to remove Shorna Akter and Ritu Moni.

Umm-e-Hani’s dismissal of Shorna for six gave her career-best T20I figures of three for 10, improving on her previous best of two for 28 against Sri Lanka in Dambulla earlier this year.

Nashra Sandhu removed Rabeya Khan for the seventh wicket with Bangladesh on 93, leaving the target beyond their reach.

Fatima also chipped in with the wicket of Ritu Moni, taking her tally to 31 wickets in T20Is in 2026.

Pakistan’s campaign had begun with a three-wicket victory over Thailand in the quarter-final before Sri Lanka beat them by eight wickets in the semi-final.

The bronze-medal victory ensured they returned home from the Asian Games with a podium finish.

India clinch gold

India routed Sri Lanka by 147 runs in the final to take home gold.

The Women in Blue batted first and posted an imposing 216-3 on the board, on the back of standout knocks by openers Smriti Mandhana (79 off 45), and Shafali Verma (48 off 29).

A stellar 22-ball-49 from wicketkeeper Richa Ghosh rescued India from a slight middle-overs wobble as Sri Lanka pulled some control back. Chamudi Prabodha, Kavisha Dilhari and Sugandika Kumari took a wicket apiece.

Sri Lanka rolled over for 69 runs, with only three batters including captain Chamari Athapaththu reaching double figures.

Deepti Sharma took three wickets for her extremely miserly spell in which she conceded just six runs in her four overs, which included a maiden. Shafali accounted for the first two wickets, and bowled at an economy rate equal to Deepti’s, conceding just three runs across the two overs she bowled.

Shree Charani and Shreyanka Patil took two wickets apiece, with the latter dismissing Kaushini Nuthyangana to seal the win, completing India’s successful defense of their 2023 gold won in Hangzhou.

Sri Lanka settled for silver to complete the podium.

item.title: Pakistan miss out on Asian Games women's cricket final as Athapaththu blitz takes Sri Lanka through. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan missed out on the Asian Games women’ cricket final as Sri Lanka captain Chamari Athapaththu’s unbeaten half century gave the side an emphatic eight-wicket victory over Fatima Sana’s charges in the semi-final at Korogi Sports Park in Nisshin, Japan on Sunday.

Chasing 178, Sri Lanka raced to 178 with 13 balls to spare, with Athapaththu finishing unbeaten on 83 off 50 balls, having struck seven fours and six sixes. Harshitha Samarawickrama was unbeaten on 17.

Pakistan had appeared to set a challenging target after posting 177 for four, with Ayesha Zafar top-scoring with 71 off 40 balls and Shawaal Zulfiqar contributing 54 off 50.

But Sri Lanka’s chase quickly turned into a one-sided affair, led by their captain’s destructive hitting as Pakistan’s bowlers struggled to contain the scoring rate.

It was Pakistan’s second defeat against Sri Lanka in 10 days after the former was knocked out of the recent Women’s Asia Cup as the latter won the tournament’s semi-final.

Sri Lanka later lost to India and will meet the Asian champions — who beat Bangladesh in the other semi-final —in the gold medal decider.

Bangladesh will take on Pakistan for the bronze medal encounter on Tuesday, the same day the final is to be played.

Brisk start

Sri Lanka made a brisk start despite opening against spin, with Imesha Dulani taking the attack to Umm-e-Hani. They reached 19 without loss after two overs before a costly third over from Momina Riasat, who conceded two no-balls and a wide.

Fatima provided Pakistan with their first breakthrough in the fifth over, having Dulani bowled for 27 off 21 balls. Sri Lanka were 39 for one at that stage.

Athapaththu, initially watchful, then accelerated spectacularly. She hit Momina for a six, four, six and four in the eighth over to take Sri Lanka to 70 for one.

The Sri Lankan captain continued her assault, striking Nashra Sandhu for two fours and a six in the 10th over. Hasini Perera joined in the acceleration, particularly against Tuba Hassan, and Sri Lanka moved to 121 for one after 13 overs, needing 57 from 42 balls.

Nashra eventually broke the partnership in the following over when Hasini, who had reached 42 off 26 balls with three fours and three sixes, was caught by Umm-e-Hani at cover. Sri Lanka were 131 for two with 47 still required from 36 deliveries.

There was little further resistance from Pakistan.

Athapaththu moved to 65 off 44 balls after Fatima’s return over went for 11, before taking 15 from Umm-e-Hani’s final over, including consecutive sixes.

Sri Lanka were 157 for two after 16 overs and needed only 21 from the final four overs.

Pakistan were also unable to hold on to a chance when Aliya Riaz dropped Athapaththu at long-off off Ayesha Zafar with the batter on 79. Athapaththu hit a four in the same over before completing the chase with two balls of the 18th over remaining.

Ayesha stars

Earlier, Pakistan’s innings had suffered an early setback when opener Gull Feroza was clean bowled by Sugandika Kumari off the second delivery.

Saira Jabeen and Shawaal steadied the innings, but Saira fell for a brisk 17 off 14 balls when Sri Lanka captain Athapaththu had her caught at deep midwicket in the sixth over.

Ayesha then joined Shawaal and took the attack to the Sri Lankan bowlers. The pair added 115 runs, with Ayesha particularly aggressive against the spin.

She reached her half-century off just 27 balls as Pakistan crossed 100 in the 12th over. Ayesha eventually fell for a 40-ball 71, including nine fours and two sixes, when a risky single resulted in a run-out at the bowler’s end in the 17th over.

Shawaal brought up her half-century from 47 balls, having struck three fours and two sixes, but was dismissed for 54 off 50 balls in the following over, caught at deep midwicket after failing to get enough power behind a shot.

Fatima provided the late impetus with an unbeaten 20 off 12 balls, including two fours and a six, while Eyman Fatima struck a four from the final delivery to take Pakistan to 177 for four.

Pakistan’s innings was also helped by several fielding lapses from Sri Lanka, who missed opportunities during the middle overs.

Kumari, Athapaththu and Kawya Kavindi took one wicket apiece for Sri Lanka, with Kumari the most economical of the three, conceding 31 runs from her four overs.

item.title: Energy disruption hits Pakistan and Bangladesh as Gulf crisis worsens. [ dawn ]
item.description:
In Dhaka, the capital of Bangladesh, Parvin Akter times her cooking to the neighbourhood’s availability of piped gas. With gas in intermittent supply as a result of a global energy crunch, she now sometimes has to wait until midnight to cook her dinner.

Even switching to an induction cooker has not helped, as power outages often leave food half-cooked.

More than 2,000 kilometres away on the other side of South Asia, in Pakistan, the government has started a fuel subsidy that went into effect on Wednesday to ease the sharp rise in fuel prices.

Vehicle owners have to register for the subsidy; however, residents have complained the programme is not working smoothly.

Mohammad Musharraf, who lives in Karachi, says he has spent days trying to register with his motorcycle and ID card number, but has struggled.

“First of all, you have to register your vehicle. Then you have to register your mobile phone. How can an illiterate person survive if the conditions are so difficult?”

Attacks by the US and Israel on Iran over six months ago led to the disruption of oil and gas exports through the Strait of Hormuz. Now fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis also imperils trade through the Red Sea.

The problems at the two chokepoints have driven Asian spot liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices back toward $30 per million British thermal units this week, the second such spike this year, from about $10 before the war.

Shell estimates the world has lost roughly 36 million tonnes of LNG from the Middle East so far this year, and the shortage is particularly hitting countries where governments have limited financial leeway to intervene.

In Bangladesh, the shortfall has triggered blackouts and factory shutdowns. Pakistan and other countries in the region are rushing to blunt public anger with hastily introduced subsidies.

Bangladesh in the dark

Bangladesh draws more than 40 per cent of its electricity from imported LNG, and disruptions in deliveries from Qatar — once the source of 95pc of those imports — have forced Dhaka to chase costlier cargoes on the spot market.

“Industrial growth is slowing down, and production is going down,” Power Minister Iqbal Hasan Mahmud said this week.

The strain shows up in orders in its garments industry, the country’s biggest export.

A survey of knitwear factories by the BKMEA trade group found 55pc had seen buyers cancel or cut orders because of gas and power shortages since late August, and 78pc had partially halted production.

At one factory, a boiler ruined in mid-process by low gas pressure forced owner Alvi Islam to source fabric from China instead — a delay that led a buyer to cut a 50,000-piece order to 40,000.

Others had to take on additional expenses after energy-related production delays forced them to send finished products by plane to meet deadlines. Garment industry executive Fazlee Shamim Ehsan said his factory had to pay $50,000 to send hoodie jackets by air freight to a French buyer.

“On top of that, we’ve had to spend extra money on diesel just to keep the factory running,” said Ehsan, who is the managing director of Fatullah Apparels Ltd.

In Tangail city, poultry farmer Sayedul Islam said power outages are killing 15 to 20 of his birds a day because he cannot run the electric fans needed to cool his sheds.

Even hospitals aren’t spared. In Sylhet, power cuts hit the local hospital almost hourly. While generators keep intensive care units running, they don’t always suffice for ward ventilation, leaving patients to cope with the heat in crowded rooms.

The government has said it is seeking solutions. Fazlul Hoque of the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry pointed to a directive to fix a non-functional LNG terminal, which would help more tankers unload.

Some, including business owner Ehsan, said they have noticed slight improvements in recent days with gas supplies increasing.

Grids and gas tanks

Pakistan’s power grid is under a milder version of the same strain.

The government has reintroduced austerity measures in an effort to conserve fuel, setting 9pm as the time for closing markets and reducing fuel provision for official vehicles by 50pc for a period of three months.

The Pakistani power sector will need up to 400m cubic feet of gas a day through winter, Independent System and Market Operator (ISMO) data shows, with only two LNG cargoes confirmed so far for September.

One standard Pakistan LNG cargo is around 140,000 cubic metres, equivalent to roughly 3 billion cubic feet of gas, or just over one week’s supply.

While solar power has eased some of Pakistan’s power crunch in recent years, the country still needs gas for other sectors and households, said Masood Nabi, chief executive of state importer Pakistan LNG, at Gastech this week.

The more immediate battle in Pakistan, though, is over transport fuel prices.

The Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme that took effect on Wednesday night offers motorcycle, rickshaw and small-car owners a subsidy of Rs100 a litre on a capped monthly quota.

Petrol has risen to roughly Rs391 ($1.41) a litre and diesel to Rs421 ($1.52) — a heavy burden in a country where the minimum wage is around $145 a month.

Business leaders and workers say it isn’t enough.

“We used to eat meat once a week, but now it is difficult to afford it even once a month,” said Amesh Gul, 32, a rickshaw driver in Karachi whose income has taken a hit with rising fuel prices.

“All I ask of the government is to please take care of poor people.”

Header image: People on motorbikes ride past a portrait of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif set up in protest against rising fuel prices, ahead of the nationwide rollout of a government fuel subsidy scheme, in Karachi on Sept 16, 2026. — Reuters
